title: Care for electronic equipment and measuring instruments

lessons.title: Electronic equipment and instruments at work
lessons.html:
Instruments we depend on

In a food factory or abattoir, many decisions depend on electronic equipment and measuring instruments. If they are wrong, the product can be unsafe or the business loses money.

Examples

InstrumentUsed for
Probe thermometerMeasuring meat or product temperature
Chiller and freezer thermometers and data loggersRecording room temperatures
ScalesWeighing carcasses, cartons and ingredients
pH meterMeasuring acidity of meat or water
Metal detectorFinding metal pieces in packed product
Handheld scanners and tabletsRecording data and barcodes
Electric stunnersStunning animals (only trained operators)

Why care matters

  • A thermometer that reads 2 degrees too low can let warm meat be despatched.
  • A scale that reads wrong means customers are over- or under-charged.
  • Broken equipment stops production.
  • Electronic equipment is expensive to replace.

Basic rules

  • Use equipment only for its purpose and as you were trained.
  • Read the instructions or ask your supervisor if unsure.
  • Never use equipment that is damaged, wet inside or shows an error.
  • Report problems at once.

Who looks after equipment?

Everyone who uses equipment must look after it. Your supervisor makes sure equipment is checked and repaired. A technician or outside company services and calibrates it. You must use it correctly, keep it clean, check it before use and report problems.

Know which instruments are used in your area and where they are kept. Learn how each one works. If a new instrument comes, ask for training before you use it. Treat instruments with care: do not drop them, throw them or leave them where they can be knocked over or stood on.

lessons.title: Using and cleaning instruments
lessons.html:
Using instruments correctly

Probe thermometers

  1. Clean and sanitise the probe before use.
  2. Push the probe into the thickest part of the meat, not touching bone.
  3. Wait until the reading is steady.
  4. Write down the reading, time and product.
  5. Clean and sanitise the probe after use, and before the next product.

Scales

  • Check the scale shows zero before you weigh. Press "zero" or "tare" if needed.
  • Put the item in the middle of the scale.
  • Do not drop heavy items on the scale.
  • Do not go over the maximum weight on the label.

Cleaning electronic equipment

  • Switch off or unplug before cleaning, if the instructions say so.
  • Do not spray water directly onto electronic parts unless the equipment is made to be washed down. Use a damp cloth and the cleaning product allowed.
  • Keep the screen and buttons clean and dry.
  • Do not use sharp objects to press buttons or scratch the screen.

Batteries and charging

  • Charge handheld devices at the charging station at the end of the shift.
  • Replace batteries in thermometers when the low battery sign shows.
  • Dispose of old batteries in the battery bin, not in general waste.

Electrical safety

  • Never touch plugs or switches with wet hands.
  • Check cables for cuts and damage. Do not use damaged cables.
  • Keep cables off wet floors where possible.

Ask for help if unsure.

Follow the instructions for each instrument, and ask your supervisor to show you how to clean it.

lessons.title: Checking, storing and reporting
lessons.html:
Is the instrument accurate?

Instruments must be checked regularly to make sure they give the right reading. This is called verification or calibration.

Simple checks you may do

  • Thermometer ice-point check: put the probe in a cup of crushed ice and a little water. After it settles, it should read about 0 °C. If it is wrong by more than your procedure allows, report it.
  • Scale check: weigh a known test weight. The scale must show the correct weight.
  • Write the result, date and your name on the check sheet.

Full calibration is done by a trained technician or an outside company, at the times set by the company. Scales used for trade may need to meet legal metrology requirements.

Storing equipment

  • Store in the case or holder provided, in a clean, dry place.
  • Do not leave instruments in hot sun, in a freezer, or on wet floors unless they are made for it.
  • Do not put heavy things on top of them.
  • Return shared equipment to its place at the end of the shift.

Reporting faults

  1. Stop using the equipment.
  2. Put a "Do not use" tag on it.
  3. Tell your supervisor what happened.
  4. Fill in the fault report or maintenance form.
  5. Use a back-up instrument if there is one.

Never open electronic equipment or try to repair it yourself unless you are trained and allowed.

Key points

  • Instruments such as thermometers and scales protect food safety and fair trade.
  • Clean and sanitise probes before and after use.
  • Check scales show zero and do not overload them.
  • Do ice-point and test-weight checks and record them.
  • Tag and report faulty equipment; do not repair it yourself.
